Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out.

It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend.

The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans).

More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains.

In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries.

Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology.

I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out.

Raw data from the physical world.

Robots need to be able to comprehend locations as they are, not as they are projected onto the earth as blueprints.

A blueprint isn't going to create a loading bay that never existed.

Roofs are well covered by existing mapping systems. Roads as well.

Interior spaces are where the disparity becomes much more glaring.

That's where @vangrid_io is aiming.

Smartphones act as the collection layer. A buyer can fund a bounty for a site. An individual on the ground slowly orbits the structure recording. The AI stack can get more involved.

The training pipeline can scale.

But none of that eliminates the fundamental requirement.

The physical geometry still needs to be collected from the physical world.

What happens when the camera collecting spatial data isn’t a Vangrid edge node?

@vangrid_io has designed for that too.

Its "/v1/ingest" API allows external sensor systems , from drones and fixed cameras to vehicle mounted cameras , to send raw video into the Vangrid pipeline.

From there, the heavy lifting happens on Vangrid’s side.

The system processes the footage, performs perception and georeferencing checks, then extracts spatial observations such as objects, vehicles and structures.

Each resulting observation receives a "provenance_hash", connecting it to @vangrid_io ’s cryptographic provenance system.

So instead of asking every sensor operator to build their own spatial-data pipeline, the workflow becomes:

Capture → Upload → Process → Extract → Verify

That’s an important piece of infrastructure if @vangrid_io wants its spatial layer to work across different types of real world sensors.

2102986253792575689.text:
When you think about spatial data, it’s easy to picture someone walking around with a phone.

But real world sensing goes much further than that.

@vangrid_io ’s ingestion layer is designed to accept video from external systems such as drones, fixed cameras and vehicle mounted cameras.

The important part is that these sources don’t need to produce finished spatial observations themselves.

They provide the footage.

@vangrid_io ’s pipeline can then handle perception, georeferencing and quality checks before extracting structured observations from the video.

Each extracted observation is also processed through Vangrid’s provenance system and receives a "provenance_hash".

That gives Vangrid a broader path to collecting spatial information:

Different sensors → one processing layer → structured spatial observations.

For a network designed around understanding the physical world, being able to work across different types of sensors is an important piece of the architecture.

Deel hit $140M ARR in 90 days. The crazy part is how much work AI can now handle behind that insane scale.

The real test of an AI agent isn’t whether it can approve a receipt.

Getting through the obvious claims faster is useful. But the messy ones are where I’d want to look closer: different country rules, multiple receipts in one upload, or an exception only one teammate knows how to handle.

I don’t want to write 100 instructions just to hand off a task I already know how to do.

I’d rather show the agent how I work, let my team fill in what I miss, and have those lessons carry into the next review.

Vanessa at Deel says she went from 500+ hours a month on expense reviews to under a few with Akai.

That’s a compelling headline.

But the bigger draw for me is not having to teach every agent, for every teammate, the same lesson again.

Less time checking routine receipts. More attention on the ones that actually need judgment.

2102754254146732252.text:
Another SaaS sell off is just inevitable at this point because of the rise of AI agents.

Goldman Sachs expects the software profit pool to shift heavily toward AI agents, with the agent market growing to more than $50 billion by 2030 while traditional SaaS falls from roughly $30 billion to around $20 billion.
This does not mean software is disappearing but the overall market could actually become larger, but more of the money is expected to move away from traditional SaaS products and toward the agents operating them.

Today, businesses pay monthly fees for employees to use Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday and dozens of other applications but agents can move across those applications and complete the work themselves. Instead of opening several programs, the user simply explains the desired outcome. The agent becomes the main interface, while the software underneath turns into a tool working quietly in the background. This puts pressure on the traditional per seat model because companies may not need as many employees actively using each application. It also weakens customer lock in because users become more loyal to the agent than to the software it operates.

Yes, I know many large software companies now offer usage based pricing alongside their legacy seat based models. That should help them adapt as customers move toward paying for completed work rather than software access but the market rarely makes that distinction during a major sell off. If investors begin dumping SaaS stocks because they fear AI agents will weaken seat growth and pricing power, even the strongest software giants will probably get grouped into the same trade and sold alongside the weaker companies. We already saw broad software weakness when new agent products raised similar concerns earlier this year.

Muse will be the next catalyst because it is bringing personal agents to a much larger audience. Once regular users become comfortable allowing one agent to work across multiple applications, investors will begin questioning how many separate subscriptions and paid seats businesses truly need. OpenAI and Anthropic will likely respond soon their own version of Muse very soon. And once Muse, OpenAI and Anthropic begin competing to control the user’s entire workflow, SaaS companies will no longer compete only against other software products but also compete against the AI agents deciding which software gets used in the first place.

Not every SaaS company will lose because those with proprietary data, deep integrations and strong usage based models should be more defensible but if another broad SaaS sell off begins, the market may not care about those differences at first. The weaker companies will fall and the giants will likely get dragged down with them.

as we use more ai to write code, and I keep encountering worlds where even if you put all the people on the team together in a room you won't have 100% "understanding coverage" (like test coverage) of the codebase, I keep going back to the Peter Naur piece of programming as theory building. 

i'll write more about this - foggy thoughts - but I see the "code is like assembly" future. it is inevitable 

when I started getting into moderately sized codebases first time in my life, most teams typically had 100% "code reading coverage" summed up across the team, not necessarily a single person. but for every part of the codebase someone in the team knew exactly what it did 

what i have seen in larger codebases (long running oss projects like linux kernel, or internal codebases of bigtech companies), is that because of the team churn, and sprawl of the codebase, you actually can find large swathes of codebase which no one in the current team has it entirely in their head. 

it didn't exactly stop these software projects from surviving or thriving or expanding further. what was different though is that regardless of shitty/elegant, the code was written by humans and do a degree hence readable by humans, so even if there are pockets of code no one knows, someone could sit with it for a couple of days and spool it up in their head 

ai changes a lot of it. the speed and volume is entirely different. we will have to 'shift up a plane' of abstraction in terms of where do we want to understand the program 

and hence Peter Naur was right that the code itself doesn't matter. the theory of the program is what matters and the team still needs to build the theory of the program in their head. the old ways will not work in the new world

AMI Labs just raised $1.03B at a $3.5B valuation to build world models.

That is a lot of money going into teaching AI how the physical world works.

What I keep wondering is what they will learn it from. @vangrid_io is working on exactly that side of the problem.

A loading bay after the equipment gets moved.

A sidewalk the week construction starts.

A stairwell at 6pm with half the lights off.

Places change constantly, and almost nobody has fresh data on them.

That is  why I am keeping an eye on this one.

You point your phone at a street. Faces and plates get blurred on the device and the raw footage never leaves it.

Buyers get the mesh, geometry, ground truth score and provenance, but not the video.

So you are buying a model of the place, not a recording of everyone who walked past.

You can also set privacy zones around your home or workplace.

No system is perfect but keeping raw footage off the server changes the risk a lot.

Labs will keep improving the brains.

Someone still has to supply real, current data about the world.

That layer is underrated and @vangrid_io is building right in it.

I’ve interviewed for these companies (sometimes more than once) over the past ~5 years. Got to the offer stage in 4 of them, and ended up working for 2.

This is a summary of my experience, top-down in classic MBB fashion👇🏼

All of these companies share these factors in how they filter talent:

Target schools, 90% GPA, extracurricular activities, experience (for non entry-level roles) and Case-interview performance. You don’t need all of them to get in, but you need to tick at least 3 of these boxes.

1. Target schools: 

The most controversial one, there is no real definition for this, it changes by firm, and by office within the same firm. But generally it looks something like this:

a) Top 30 schools in NA and EU
b) Top 3-5 schools in your country 
    b1) in KSA that would be KFUPM, KSU,          MBSC, KAU and Alfaisal University 

2. 90% GPA:

Self explanatory, take your GPA format (5.0 or 4.0) and x0.9 - this is your target.

3. Extracurricular Activities: 

Non of the “managed a book club, head of student council, barista at Starbucks” bullshit. Consulting internships, consulting competitions, hackathons, etc. Are what matters most.

4. Experience (for experienced hires):

Prior MBB experience is a massive plus, but not your only way in. “Unique” experience is what they look for in professionals who are shifting from industry. 

An ex-founder with a startup that failed before Series-B is more in-demand than an accountant in some commercial bank. 

5. Case interview performance: 

This is where most people fail. 

A bizzare brain teaser like “how many gas stations are in Riyadh” or “How many tooth brushes are in Dubai” may seem like an arbitrary question that measures nothing. It isn’t. It measures how quickly can you sort this problem into clean buckets and identify its drivers. Your contextual assumptions, your math, your final answer don’t matter. Only your ability to structure your thoughts does. 

And let’s be honest, it’s also a way to measure how quickly you can bullshit your way into a plausible-sounding answer when you’re put on the spot by a client.

As for the case itself, https://t.co/c7GHn0aDF7 is your best friend. Target solving 2 cases of each type CORRECTLY -however many tries it takes you- before interviewing.

I hope this is helpful to you whether you’re a student, fresh grad, or an experienced professional looking into shifting your career.

And thanks to @The_Lazy_Nerd for starting this.

Thrilled to announce our latest incubation: Horowitz Andreessen Academy.

Horowitz Andreessen Academy will be a two-year residential program in San Francisco for 16 to 22 year olds.

My biggest regret from my college experience is how divorced it was from the real world (both practically but also intellectually)

HAA is the opposite. Students will learn from real-world practitioners and intellectuals; including founders (Sam Altman, Brian Armstrong, Jensen Huang), investors (Elad Gil, Daniel Gross), and professors (Agnes Callard, Tyler Cowen), among hundreds of others. The Academy is the educational experience I wish I had.

In 1984, the educational psychologist Benjamin Bloom published a paper about how the average student who received one-on-one tutoring focused on mastery techniques performed better than 98% of the control group. For generations, this was viewed as unrealistic to implement even if it produced the best outcomes.

At the Academy, we will be able to locate any tutor on any topic that a student desires.

Take an aspiring filmmaker or producer. The standard path offers them film theory courses, peer workshops, and the occasional visiting filmmaker; everything past that takes meticulous networking and luck. The very entrepreneurial type will find ways to invite prominent speakers to speak and meticulous networking to reach the right people. At the Academy, they will learn the business from the people who run it and their next creative project will have notes from award-winning filmmakers.

Take a young founder. Yes, there is endless content online; you can watch a video on any skill. But content is not coaching. The Academy will provide dedicated, experienced coaches and mentors who know your company and psychology. Students can workshop issues with prominent leaders in technology who host sessions on campus. Every generation of entrepreneurs has had mentors in their corner. Ours will too.

Take the technical student focused on research. At the Academy, academics are focused on the frontier. Students will be taught and mentored by AI researchers at frontier labs. They’ll be conducting research and sharing progress, and presenting their work at ICML and ICLR. 

The goal of the Academy is to identify the right mentors, the correct bottlenecks, and the right introductions, adjusted continuously around one person and their pursuits.

The education philosophy focuses on co-ops, courses, and pursuits.

Co-ops are the opportunity to work during the year (not just over the summer). It's the chance to work across countless different roles and companies, including getting connected to our 10 founding partners: Anduril, Anthropic, Coinbase, Google, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAI, Palantir, Replit, and Stripe.

Courses are taught by legendary people: people who have founded unicorns, invested in those unicorn companies, or are on the intellectual frontier.

And most importantly, it's about Pursuits. It's about personal projects, quests, startup ideas, rabbit holes that define the student experience. The Academy will provide dedicated, experienced coaches and mentors who know your work and psychology.

At HAA, the individual education of each student is the whole design. We want to meet you. Applications for the founding class are open.

Release Notes

Version 1.0.41 — September 22, 2026

Features

MiMo-V2.6: The Hard Road to Scaling Up RL

MiMo-V2.6 is very likely one of the largest single RL runs, by compute, that any open-source model team has undertaken to date. In an era when compute is brutally scarce, we still chose to dedicate a team of several dozen people to one goal over an extended period: scaling up RL. That takes more than research conviction. It takes a vision for AGI, respect for the unknown, and the nerve to walk straight into the hardest problems.

The result is a model whose potential was built through mid-training and unlocked through heavy RL. Today, it is the number one open-source model. I strongly recommend reading the technical report. I believe it will become one of those papers that Agent RL practitioners keep reopening and discovering something new in each time. In my view, the research innovations and engineering challenges behind it surpass those of DeepSeek R1, which I was partly involved in.

Some will ask: why MixRL instead of MOPD? First, they are not competing choices. We ran MixRL on verifiable tasks of moderate difficulty, including code and related agentic tasks, and found that the resulting models generalize remarkably well. Second, tasks that are difficult to verify, extremely long-horizon, or simply too challenging to include in a joint RL run are trained separately. Including them would substantially reduce rollout efficiency or introduce significant rollout staleness. We then merge the resulting capabilities through MOPD. Games, 3D tasks, and tasks with subjective evaluation signals all fall into this category.

There is also a third, slightly cheeky answer. Our team is flat enough and free enough of organizational silos that MixRL simply is not difficult for us. More importantly, everyone enjoys working this way. People from different domains come together every day, driven by the pursuit of AGI and intelligence that can continuously improve itself, to confront and resolve the RL bottlenecks in each field. I will always remember the RL daily update meetings from this period. They were intense and dense, with intelligence emerging in real time.

To help the open-source community focus on solving real Agentic RL problems, we have released a Qwen model distilled from MiMo RL trajectories as a stronger starting point for RL, along with 7K diverse environments and a complete RL training framework. We hope these resources will help move Agentic RL research forward.

MiMo-V2.6 is only the beginning. In an era when intelligence is easy to replicate, we still choose the hard road toward self-improvement and AGI. Much of what lies ahead remains unknown. But we are willing to keep investing the time, compute, and passion required to take on one hard problem after another and work each of them all the way through, until intelligence crosses into a new regime.

2102820148629614685.text:
Muse, Instinct, OpenClaw, Claude Code…
All successful agents have 3 key components:

🧠 Brain → model, harness (logic)
👐 Hands → tools, computer, browser
🗃️ Files → memories, skills, repos

The 'easy' way is to throw all these in 1 stateful computer (a Mac Mini)

Like, you run 𝚌𝚕𝚊𝚞𝚍𝚎 or 𝚏𝚡 in your mac, you keep it running all day with 𝚌𝚊𝚏𝚏𝚎𝚒𝚗𝚊𝚝𝚎, it has storage, and CLIs and apps installed.

But if you want to cost-efficiently run agents in the cloud, you actually start breaking down these parts.

🧠 The harness can run in Fluid compute. To make it reliable across restarts, rollouts, crashes, you make its event log durable using Workflow.

👐 The hands can be a dedicated browser fleet like Browserbase/Kernel, a computer like Sandbox, and even more efficient lightweight tools like just-bash.

🗃️ 🆕 What was missing was a way to also decouple storage. Imagine you want to run a memory consolidation cron job every night ("dreaming"). You can read/write to the files directly without 'booting up' the agent's full computer.

Today we're introducing the perfect companion to Sandbox: Drives. We shipped the computer for agents, now we're giving you the 'external disk' you can attach at will. It's early, and we'll be expanding capabilities here quickly.

Btw, breaking apart the agent into these independent parts not only optimizes costs in a big way, it also *massively* improves security and auditability. I'd argue you can't even run a secure agent otherwise!

2102163474709389562.text:
how to improve GPT-6 Astra / Codex's ability to design and code websites

I've been using this approach since GPT Image was released, and the results have kept improving with 2 and 2.5

the idea is to have Codex generate visual mockups of the website before building it, whether you're reimagining an existing page or starting with an idea from scratch

you can review the layout, give feedback and agree on the design before it starts writing the frontend

here's how to use it:

1. give Codex the idea and your context

explain who the website is for, what it needs to communicate and what you want someone to do when they visit

include the material you already have:

> your page copy and product information
> brand guidelines, fonts, colors and assets
> screenshots of the existing page if you're redesigning
> references with notes on what you like about each one

have it ask about anything missing before generating the mockup

for an existing website, ask it to inspect the current implementation too, including components and functionality that need to stay

2. ask it to generate the design first

be explicit that you want an image mockup to review before implementation

a starting prompt:

> use imagegen to create a website mockup from this brief and the attached references
> use the supplied copy, brand assets and product information
> show the page layout, typography, imagery and calls to action, and wait for my feedback before writing code

you can request different visual directions if you're still exploring, with each version changing something meaningful like the layout or use of imagery

3. work through the mockup together

review it as a page someone needs to understand and use

> is the main message clear?
> does the layout guide attention toward the intended action?
> is the text readable?
> does the design fit your brand?
> are there generic sections or invented details that should be removed?

give specific feedback on the image, such as increasing the space around the headline, reducing decorative elements or moving the product example higher on the page

ask it to revise the chosen mockup while preserving the parts you've approved

4. turn the approved mockup into a build plan

have Codex identify the sections, reusable components and assets needed to implement the design

agree on what happens when someone interacts with it, including navigation, forms, buttons and any loading or error states

also define how the layout should adapt to mobile, because a desktop mockup leaves those decisions open

save the approved image and your decisions in the project so Codex can refer to them during the build

5. find relevant UX / UI skills before building

you can find these in skill directories and through recommendations on X, UI Skills is one example to explore

https://t.co/NSjtzraOfs

give your Grok Bot the project brief and have it research which skills are popular and worth considering for your stack

ask it to check what each skill does, who maintains it and whether its instructions fit the website you're building

that could include skills for:

> frontend design and component patterns
> accessibility and responsive layouts
> animation and interaction design
> reviewing the finished UI

review the shortlist, then give Codex the selected skills alongside your design system and approved mockup before implementation

6. build the page from that reference

ask Codex to implement the approved design using your project's existing stack and components where appropriate

keep headings, buttons and forms as working website elements, with illustrations and other generated visuals saved as separate assets

a useful implementation prompt:

> build the approved mockup as a responsive page
> preserve its layout, spacing, typography and visual hierarchy, use the approved copy and implement the interactions we agreed

I think it's time to hang up my Three.js hat.

First of all, this is not a pity post—I'll be fine. I'm also not 100% confident about this.

But I'm an over-sharer and like to talk out loud, so I thought I would share some thoughts on where I see things going and why I'm considering quitting Three.js development.

Some signals I've noticed lately that have gotten me thinking:
- Since Astra was released, I've probably seen at least 10 posts from different people that have achieved similar quality to Three.js Water Pro or better.
- Someone downloaded a video recording of one my posts, fed it to Astra and recreated it with 90% accuracy
- I've had less and less clients referrals
- A Three.js developer I respect very much is retiring from the industry due to impact of AI and lack of interest
- I've heard 2nd hand accounts of other developers losing majority of course/plugin sales due to AI
- I've noticed Three.js posts have shifted from work created by seasoned developers to vibe-coded games and demos.

Fundamentally, I no longer really see value in what I do when it can be replicated so easily.

I've always enjoyed working on hard problems. Naturally, outsourcing the hard part to an agent takes away a lot of the enjoyment for me. High-level orchestration of agents does not tickle my brain in any special way.

At the end of most days I feel unfulfilled and bored. I honestly feel like I've lost much of my critical thinking ability as I've stopped coding. I find it harder to focus on tasks and my attention-span and comprehension is noticeably dropping.

My plan right now is to finish up Water Pro v4 and see how that performs. After that, I think it's time to start thinking about what else is out there for me.

I'd love to hear thoughts from other developers & freelancers on the matter, positive or negative.

Feel free to vent!

Been testing Claude Opus 5.5 for Google Ads since it dropped and gotta say this model is cracked...

(Can’t believe they beat Fable 5.1 on EVERY benchmark and priced it at half the cost.)

So here's a 10-stage AI workflow to automate 80% of your Google Ads with it:

(Literally every prompt you'll need. Save this)

Stage 0: Build the project brain

Before asking for anything, create a Claude Project and feed it everything.

- Product pages
- Best sellers
- Customer reviews
- Objection docs
- Competitor URLs
- Meta ads
- Google Ads Transparency Center links
- Search terms reports
- Winning ad copy
- Offer details
- Brand guidelines
- Past landing pages
- Performance exports

Then run this prompt:

"Act as the Google Ads strategy brain for this brand. Read all uploaded context and create a working brand profile covering: ICP, core pain points, buying triggers, objections, emotional language customers use, top products, strongest offers, competitor positioning, current funnel gaps, and Google Ads opportunities. Do not make recommendations yet. First summarise the context and ask me what is missing."

The quality of the outputs you'll get from this AI workflow will directly correlate with the quality of the context you give it here.

And Opus 5.5 makes this the cheapest it's ever been to run because they made this model forget way less context than what it used to. 

Stage 1: Customer language mining

"Search Reddit, YouTube comments, Amazon reviews, TikTok comments, and niche forums for people discussing problems related to [PRODUCT CATEGORY]. Extract the exact words they use when describing the problem, what they have tried, why those solutions failed, what outcome they want, and what would make them buy. Format this as: Quote / Pain Point / Desired Outcome / Funnel Stage / Possible Ad Angle."

This gives you the language that keyword tools would never show you.

If someone writes:

"I'm tired of wasting money on supplements that do nothing."

That can be a winning ad angle right there.

(And research is where 5.5 quietly embarrasses everything else. It surpasses every Mythos class model somehow.)

Stage 2: Competitor angle map

"Research these competitors: [COMPETITOR 1], [COMPETITOR 2], [COMPETITOR 3]. Use Google Ads Transparency Center, Meta Ad Library, their landing pages, product pages, offers, guarantees, reviews, and email capture flows. Build a table showing: offer, main promise, ad hooks, landing page angle, proof used, objections handled, pricing position, and what they are NOT saying."

Then run:

"Based on this competitor research, identify the 5 most validated market angles and the 5 biggest white-space angles we can own. For each angle, explain which funnel stage it belongs to and what campaign type should test it first."

If 3 competitors are all running the same hook, that angle is validated.

You don't even need to be original. Just add your unique spin to what's already working.

Stage 3: Keyword research

"Using the customer language, competitor research, product pages, and search intent data, build a full Google Ads keyword universe for [BRAND]. Split it into: branded, competitor, high-intent product, problem-aware, solution-aware, comparison, ingredient/material, use-case, gift/occasion, and negative keywords. For each keyword, include funnel stage, intent level, match type, campaign/ad group recommendation, and landing page angle."

Then run:

"Now prioritise this keyword research report into a 30-day launch plan. Separate must-launch keywords from phase 2 tests. Flag any keywords that are high volume but low commercial intent."

This stops the campaign from becoming a messy keyword dump.

Stage 4: Campaign architecture

"Turn the finalized keyword research report into a complete Google Ads account structure. Include campaign names, ad group names, keyword match types, bidding strategy, starting budget split, exclusions, negative keyword rules, and when each campaign should launch. Use this structure: branded search, branded shopping, non-branded shopping, non-branded search, competitor search, PMax remarketing with brand exclusions, display remarketing, Demand Gen, and TOF search tests."

Then add:

"Explain why each campaign exists, what signal it is meant to produce, and what metric decides whether it scales, holds, or gets cut."

Every campaign needs to play a role in your ecosystem. If it doesn't, you should just stop running it.

Stage 5: RSA copy production

"Write responsive search ad copy for [PRODUCT] targeting [KEYWORD]. Funnel stage: [BOF/MOF/TOF]. Use the customer language and competitor gap analysis above. Give me 15 headlines under 30 characters and 4 descriptions under 90 characters. Include: benefit-led headlines, problem-led headlines, proof-led headlines, offer-led headlines, and urgency-led headlines. Make sure headline 1 matches the search intent."

Then run:

"Create 3 ad variations for this keyword: one direct-response version, one proof-heavy version, and one problem-agitation version. Explain which audience each variation is for."

BOF copy should sound like the product is the obvious answer.

MOF copy should make the benefit feel believable.

TOF copy should make the problem impossible to ignore.

This is the stage where 5.5 earns its keep btw. Anthropic rebuilt how it writes: no jargon, no idiosyncratic AI phrases, and it FOLLOWS the writing rules you give it. It really writes the way you do. Give it your banned words list once and your ads stop needing the de-AI editing pass.

Stage 6: Merchant Center feed optimization

"Rewrite this product title for Google Shopping using the structure: Brand + Product Type + Core Keyword + Key Feature + Use Case/Benefit. Stay under 150 characters. Give me 10 variations ranked by likely search intent."

Then:

"Write a Merchant Center description for [PRODUCT]. Use up to 5,000 characters. Include all relevant buyer keywords naturally, cover features, benefits, use cases, materials/ingredients, sizing/specs, objections, and reasons to choose this product. Do not include irrelevant keywords or products we do not sell."

Then:

"Audit this product feed for missed Google Shopping opportunities. Check title, description, product type, Google product category, images, variants, pricing, promotions, shipping, reviews, and attributes. Tell me exactly what to change."

Stage 7: Landing page angles

"Build a landing page brief for [PRODUCT] targeting people searching [KEYWORD]. Awareness stage: [PROBLEM-AWARE/SOLUTION-AWARE/PRODUCT-AWARE]. Structure it as: hero headline, subheadline, proof bar, problem section using customer language, mechanism section, product section, comparison section, reviews, objection handling, FAQ, CTA. Make sure the first screen matches the search query."

Then run:

"Create 5 landing page angle variations for this product based on different search intents. For each one, give me the hero, core promise, proof required, objections to handle, and CTA."

Send the best one into Claude Code.

Now you have an intent-specific page created instead of 1 generic PDP trying to convert everyone.

And the pages come out looking GOOD - both design and copywise.

Stage 8: Creative production

Connect Higgsfield MCP inside Claude.

Then run:

"Create a 9-shot YouTube ad concept for [PRODUCT] based on this angle: [ANGLE]. Style can be claymation / UGC / cinematic product demo. For each shot, include scene description, voiceover, on-screen text. Use GPT Images 2.0 for the statics."

Then:

"Create 5 new creative concepts from the strongest customer pain points in the research. Each concept should include hook, visual metaphor, script, image prompts, animation prompts, and CTA."

If you wanna run video ads, animate your statics with Seedance 2.5

Use Opus 5.5 to write the scripts. Voiceovers read human now, not like a LinkedIn post.

Shouldn't cost more than $3 per ad.

Stage 9: Daily campaign audit

Connect Google Ads MCP (or just export report CSV)

Then run:

"Pull the last 7 days of Google Ads performance and compare it to the previous 7 days. For each campaign show spend, revenue, ROAS, conversions, CPA, CPC, CTR, impression share, search lost IS rank, search lost IS budget, and top search terms. Flag: ROAS down 20%+, CPA up 20%+, budget-limited winners, rank-limited campaigns, branded leakage in non-branded campaigns, wasted spend queries, and products spending with no conversions."

Next up:

"Turn this audit into an action list. For each action, include the campaign, issue, evidence, recommended change, risk level, and expected impact."

Stage 10: Weekly scaling plan

"Compare performance across 7, 14, and 30-day windows. Identify campaigns, products, keywords, ads, and landing pages with consistent green signals. Recommend which budgets to increase by 15-20%, which to hold, which to decrease, and which tests to launch next. Do not recommend scaling anything unless the signal is consistent across multiple windows."

Then:

"Create next week's testing roadmap. Include 3 keyword tests, 3 creative tests, 2 landing page tests, 2 feed tests, and 1 campaign structure test. Rank them by expected impact and implementation difficulty."

And 5.5 is the model I trust most running this unattended. 

Anthropic's behavioral audit scored it their safest model to date, way less likely to take hard-to-reverse actions than anything before it. 

Exactly what you want from the thing reading your account every morning.

And this is how you get your full ecosystem set up:

- Research feeds keywords
- Keywords feed campaigns
- Campaign data feeds landing pages
- Landing pages feed creative
- Creative feeds new angles
- Audits feed the next week of tests

A better brain than Fable 5.1, a smaller bill, and copy that ships without the AI smell.

(If you want me to build this full AI Google Ads production system for your brand btw, DM me "OPUS" and I'll show you what it'd look like)

2102039765830738212.text:
New essay for @every, by @afterimage 

We believe we will look back on Astra as a turning point in how creatives use AI in video work.

For many months we were experimenting with different AI video approaches: generative workflows in ComfyUI, procedural animation with Python, motion design through the Cavalry and After Effects MCPs, and more. 

All of these were fundamentally limited by a lack of control. Generative models could sometimes make cool images, but changing one thing without disturbing everything else was difficult. 

Many of these generative tools weren't (and still aren't) built for true professional workflows. 

On the other hand, general models starting around Opus 4.5 were decent at writing python code to deterministically edit images and videos, but the models were really bad at “seeing” the images and videos they were supposed to be editing, which made them impractical.

The day Astra launched, just from the rumors and marketing, our internal sense was "this might be the one". Then, when we saw the level of 3D detail people were able to achieve with Astra in Blender, we really suspected the model was finally able to "see" and iterate toward things that actually looked good. 

While everyone raced to build cool (but often useless) demos of 3D worlds, we got interested in something else: compositing 3D assets into live action footage at commercial-grade quality. To this day, we are quite surprised by how few Astra demos focus on this ability. It feels like a breakthrough for us.

We tested a range of processes, from traditional VFX skills like masking and tracking to hybrid approaches like compositing Blender renders and generative imagery with real footage.

At the highest levels, Astra doesn’t replace someone with true domain expertise in VFX artistry. But, through these tests, it started to feel for the first time that the LLM was actually a viable tool in the kit. It worked well in concert with other tools to make professional results we could actually see ourselves using.

The coolest part about all this is that it makes it easy and painless to attempt visual effects on even the smallest projects and most off the cuff videos. We’re excited about the combination of casual footage and visual maximalism. Effects can now be completely over the top without feeling like the whole reason a shot exists.

Brand has to start with the founders, not the CMO.

A lot of people ask me how @Clay built its brand and how they should be thinking about their own company's brand. The advice I give always comes back to this: brand starts at the top and has to be authentic to the founders.

There's a lot of data that shows CMOs are the most likely executive to get fired. And because of that, no matter how much they want to, they're not incentivized to take huge bets on something that won't show returns for a long time (if ever) — which is what brand is. 

Many think of marketing ROI as "how much did I put in, how much did I get out?" Brand is how much you put in today so that when you spend a dollar on performance marketing two years from now, you get more out of it. You're investing without knowing the direct ROI.

We've been investing in brand since before we had revenue - that's when we bought https://t.co/eiq4KvfSr9, hired a claymation artist to design the images below, and more. People ask me why and I wish I could say it's because I'm a marketing savant. But the truth is that we just wanted to. We wanted the brand to feel a certain way - to capture the beauty of a product that exuded flexibility and creativity - and it felt right to invest in it from the start.

Brand only works if it's authentic - and that only happens and actually gets prioritized when it comes from the top. 

As a little blast from the past, I pulled some mockups Hudson (said claymation artist) made for us ahead of our Product Hunt launch in Jan '22.

2102876778390061263.text:
I am genuinely worried that Google could lose the internet’s most valuable tollbooth over the next several years if it does not get its act together.

Amazon blocking Meta’s Muse agent is a huge warning about where the internet is heading. Amazon publicly cited privacy, security and authorization concerns but it also acknowledged that outside agents can bypass parts of its personalized shopping experience. Amazon is developing its own shopping agents, so allowing Muse to control product discovery and purchasing could hand Meta the most valuable part of the transaction, the customer relationship. That is the real battle in an agentic world. Today, people search for something, scroll through advertisements, open several links, compare their options and complete the transaction themselves. Tomorrow, a person will simply tell an AI agent what they want and let it research the products, compare prices and complete the purchase.

The agent could collapse ten searches, several advertisements and multiple website visits into a single conversation. That threatens every business that makes money by standing between a consumer’s question and the final transaction, but nobody has more to lose than Google. Google generated $60.4 billion from Search and other advertising during the first quarter of 2026, representing roughly 55% of Alphabet’s total revenue. Total Google advertising revenue reached approximately $77.3 billion, or around 70% of the company’s revenue.

Google’s business works because billions of high intent searches create valuable advertising inventory. Advertisers bid to appear when someone searches for a credit card, hotel, insurance policy, restaurant or product because those users are often close to spending money. If consumers begin asking Muse to make those decisions for them, Google does not merely lose a search, itcan lose the advertisement, the click, the behavioral data and eventually the transaction. Amazon’s decision to block Muse shows that the largest internet companies understand this danger. The company controlling the agent can decide which products get recommended, which merchants receive the order and which payment system processes the transaction. That position could eventually become more valuable than owning the website the agent visits.

Google Search currently looks stronger than ever. The chart shows Search revenue growth accelerating from 9.8% in early 2025 to 19.1% in early 2026, while Alphabet subsequently reported that first-quarter Search revenue increased 19% to $60.4 billion. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode are increasing Search usage rather than cannibalizing it and management reported that queries reached an all time high. However, the financial damage from a platform shift often appears after consumer behavior has already begun changing. AI generated answers are already reducing the need to click traditional search results. One 2026 study found that the first organic result’s click through rate fell from 20.02% to 9.69% when an AI Overview appeared, while a randomized field experiment found that AI Overviews reduced outbound organic clicks by 38%. Organic clicks are not the same as paid advertisements, so this does not prove that Google’s advertising revenue is about to collapse. However, it demonstrates the broader behavioral shift, users increasingly receive an answer without visiting the underlying websites. Agents take that shift one step further by completing the action without requiring the user to browse at all.

Google therefore faces an uncomfortable conflict. It must replace traditional Search with a more direct AI experience before competitors do, but every query it converts into one synthesized answer creates fewer obvious places to display the familiar list of advertisements. Google can insert advertisements into AI Mode and build agent driven shopping tools, but it still needs to prove that one AI conversation can monetize as effectively as an entire search results page. If it cannot, AI could improve the user experience while weakening the economics of the business.

Google clearly understands the threat, but it does not feel like the company is setting the direction of the consumer AI market. ChatGPT owns much of the mindshare, Claude is becoming a leading platform for coding and professional work, and Meta’s Muse is showing early momentum as an agent that can move across applications and complete real tasks. Google has Gemini and enormous distribution but it still has not produced a consumer agent with the same cultural momentum. It often feels like Google is responding to the industry rather than forcing everyone else to respond to it. The talent losses make this concern more serious. Over the past year, 25% of departing DeepMind researchers and advanced engineers reportedly moved to Anthropic, 21% went to Meta and 14% joined OpenAI. DeepMind’s ratio of arrivals to departures reportedly fell from approximately 12 to 1 in 2023 to roughly 2 to 1 in 2026.. Those departures reportedly include Gemini co-lead Noam Shazeer, AlphaFold leader and Nobel laureate John Jumper, and Gemini contributors Jonas Adler and Alexander Pritzel.

Google still possesses some of the strongest assets in technology because it owns Android, Chrome, Search, YouTube, Gmail, Maps, Google Pay, Cloud and one of the world’s most accomplished AI research organizations. Those products give Gemini distribution, personal context and transaction capabilities that most competitors cannot reproduce. The problem is that Google must use those advantages while protecting an extraordinarily profitable advertising machine. I interviewed every person we hired at @Clay in my orgs until we passed 300 people. 

We're scaling beyond that now, so our recruiting ops team built a system that keeps me involved in every hire. 

We have a Slack channel called hiring-theses and I review it every day. Before we hire anyone, the hiring manager writes a hiring thesis about the candidate. It answers four questions:

1. Why should we hire this person?
2. What is one exceptional thing this candidate has accomplished in their career or otherwise?
3. What are the risks/concerns?
4. How will we support this person if they join?

A thesis draws on a deep dive interview into the candidate's whole story, behavioral interviews, scored feedback from every round, and thorough reference calls. The thesis also includes every piece of submitted interviewer feedback. When I review that feedback, I notice discrepancies, pieces of feedback from an interviewer that the hiring manager didn't address, or missing voices I want to hear from. 

Then I approve, deny or discuss with the hiring team. I can't sit in every interview anymore, but I still read every thesis and every piece of feedback before someone joins Clay. 

Hopefully this is helpful to other teams scaling past the point where a founder can meet every candidate. Let me know if you have any questions!

If you didn’t know, you can use your 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 from Codex.

That means Astra can coordinate 𝘂𝗽 𝘁𝗼 𝟭𝟬 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗲𝗿𝘀 through Herdr, all running Opus 5.

Hand off the heavy implementation work to Claude Code, including polishing your pages’ layout, interactions, and visual details.

Set it up once. Here’s how 👇

1. Open Codex Desktop and install Herdr and its Skill

Select Astra and ask it to run these two commands (Mac):

brew install herdr
npx skills add herdrdev/herdr --skill herdr -g

Once installed, have Astra confirm that both Codex and Claude Code can find the Skill.

𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲𝘅 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗸𝘁𝗼𝗽. Herdr manages Claude Code in the background, so you don’t have to switch interfaces.

2. Have Astra finish the setup

Paste this prompt:

“Use the official Herdr docs and the Skill we just installed to create a coordination Skill called herdr-desktop. Keep the main conversation in Codex Desktop and use the Herdr CLI to manage background workers. Don’t require me to operate inside a Herdr terminal.

Start a separately named Herdr background session for this task, explicitly targeting the session and working directory. Check whether Claude Code CLI is installed. If it’s missing, install it. If authentication is needed, ask me to sign in.

After authentication, start one Opus 5 worker with reasoning effort explicitly set to xhigh. Give it a read-only task: inspect the project and explain its main entry points. Wait for it to finish and read back its actual response to confirm that task dispatch and result retrieval work. If the model or configuration is unavailable, tell me. Don’t silently substitute another.

Save the verified startup, dispatch, wait, and result-reading procedures in the Skill. Don’t modify project code during setup.”

3. Sign in to your Claude Code account

Astra will check Claude Code’s login status.

If needed, follow the prompts to authenticate with the account you use for your Claude Code subscription.

After that, you keep assigning tasks in Codex Desktop, while Claude Code runs in the background using that Claude account’s allowance.

4. Tell Astra how to delegate

Paste this prompt:

“From now on, use this workflow:

You are the coordinator.

→ Handle project understanding, planning, task decomposition, integration, and final review.

→ When a task needs substantial implementation, debugging, test fixes, or multi-file changes, delegate it to Claude Code through herdr-desktop. For frontend work, have it refine the layout, visual details, and actual interactions.

Use Opus 5 for workers, with reasoning effort explicitly set to xhigh.

Briefly explain the division of work, then start independent tasks in parallel. Choose concurrency based on the task, machine load, and available allowance, up to 10 workers. You don’t need to use all 10.

Give each task a clear objective, working directory, necessary context, deliverable, and completion criteria. Use separate worktrees for parallel code changes. You own the integration.

Send follow-up feedback to the original worker whenever possible and continue its existing conversation. Don’t start over every round.

After a worker finishes, inspect the actual changes yourself and run the necessary checks after integration. For page changes, open the browser and check them. When independent review would help, have another worker review the work.

Don’t treat a task as finished just because another agent says it is.

At the end, show me the result, what was verified, and any unresolved issues. Release task resources that are no longer needed while preserving the work and records needed to continue.”

A few tips:

1. Save the delegation instructions from step 4 in herdr-desktop too, so you can invoke the Skill at the start of future tasks.

2. Pair the Skill with a clear end goal. For example: “Finish this pricing page, keep it consistent with the existing site, and check the mobile layout and plan switching.”

3. Each account still has its own usage limits. Adjust concurrency to the task and remaining allowance.

4. For long tasks, keep a record of progress, key decisions, and next steps. When switching conversations, check the actual state before continuing.

It works the other way around, too: Claude Code coordinates, and Codex executes. Swap the roles and their corresponding settings.

Early takeaways from Austin Deep Tech Week: 

1. Austin is a serious f*cking city.

SF is still the center of gravity.

LA has built an absolute monster around aerospace, defense and industrials.

But after spending a few days in Austin, I'm increasingly convinced this city has structural advantages that the coasts underestimate.

People I've met here seem to have one primary objective:

Build.

Heads down. Gas pedal pinned to the floor.

Noticeably less obsession with looking important and more obsession with actually making shit work.

Deep tech rewards exactly that mentality.

2. Texas being aggressively pro-business isn't some Twitter talking point. It's an actual competitive advantage.

Heard versions of this repeatedly from founders and investors this week.

Permitting. Regulation. Taxes. Energy. Land. Manufacturing. Expansion.

When you're building software, you can abstract yourself away from geography.

When you're building atoms, geography becomes part of your cap table.

Every additional month waiting on a facility, permit, power connection or expansion is effectively dilution.

Texas understand that speed matters.

3. The coastal migration isn't over.

SF and LA still have unbelievable technical talent density, particularly at the earliest stages.

But the requirements change when a deep tech company starts working.

Now you need 100,000 square feet.

Power.

Testing.

Manufacturing.

Suppliers.

Technicians.

Hundreds of employees.

Suddenly Texas starts looking a hell of a lot more attractive.

And founders here don't seem nearly as worried about convincing talent to follow them as outsiders assume.

4. The next chapter isn't companies moving to Texas. It's companies starting here.

Historically the playbook has often been:

Coast → prove technology → raise capital → expand into Texas.

I think that increasingly becomes:

Texas → Texas → Texas.

More technical founders will move here before starting the company.

More pre-seed and seed companies will originate here.

More headquarters will be planted here from Day 1.

And that's when the flywheel gets interesting:

Talent → startups → capital → exits → experienced operators → new startups.

Once that loop starts compounding, ecosystems become very difficult to stop.

5. Austin feels significantly less distracted.

There is obviously bullshit everywhere. Startups attract grift like flies to shit.

But there's noticeably less keeping-up-with-the-Joneses energy here.

Less worrying about who raised what round.

Less optimizing for appearances.

Less obsession with which VC follows you or which dinner you got invited to.

More:

Does the thing actually work?

That cultural difference matters more than people realize.

6. “But the capital is on the coasts” is becoming a lazy argument.

Have you ever heard of a f*cking airplane?

It's 2026.

If you're building a generational company in Austin and a great investor in SF wants into the round, they're getting on the plane.

Great companies don't travel to capital.

Capital travels to great companies.

Austin already has serious institutional capital on the ground alongside a growing ecosystem of smaller funds.

More capital will follow the companies.

It always does.

7. Austin increasingly looks built for where deep tech is going, not where venture has been.

Deep tech is becoming less about a handful of scientists sitting in a Bay Area lab and increasingly about deploying massive amounts of physical infrastructure.

Factories.

Energy.

Robotics.

Defense.

Space.

Advanced manufacturing.

Data centers.

Industrial systems.

Those businesses eventually collide with the physical world.

And the physical world cares about land, power, regulation, labor, logistics and speed.

Texas has a lot of all six.

SF still has the deepest venture ecosystem. LA has built an extraordinary deep tech machine.

But Austin doesn't need to become either of them.

It may be building something fundamentally different:

A startup ecosystem optimized not just for inventing hard technology — but for actually industrializing it.

That's a much more interesting proposition.

Came into Austin Deep Tech Week thinking this was an important emerging hard tech ecosystem.

Now thinking “emerging” might already be outdated.

Ingredients are here.

Talent is coming.

Capital will follow.

Unlike a lot of startup ecosystems I've visited, Austin feels like it actually wants you to build shit here.

That's a hell of a tailwind 🏭🇺🇸

Finally - mad props @Andercot, @CaitlinCloud9, @Jason_A_Scharf + many others for putting this together & making this a kickass week!

Startups are beautiful things designed to fight the inertia of the world, but they die if the world stands still. i have a 1 y/o son, and with how fast AI is moving, it's just impossible not to wonder what his education will look like.

it's completely obvious the traditional education model is outdated and about to get disrupted in a massive way.

so i've been thinking a lot about the things i ideally want in my son's future schooling:

> a personalized-to-him AI tutor

if something comes naturally to him, let him breeze through it. if he's struggling, explain it using examples from things he's interested in, so it holds his attention and actually makes sense to him.

i think hed learn so much faster that way (instead of being stuck at the same pace as every other 8-year-old just because they were born in the same year)

> critical thinking, especially around AI.

i want him to get comfortable asking "how do we know that's true?" whether it's something AI tells him, something he reads online, or even something i tell him. then learn to look for evidence before deciding what he believes.

i want him to learn to write without AI too, because putting his own thoughts into words is part of learning how to think

i also want him to learn to sit with difficult problems before asking AI to solve them

> learning by building things.

i think @nateliason's founders school in nyc is an awesome example of this. students build their own businesses with the goal of $1M profit before graduation. i want my son getting out into the world, testing his ideas, making mistakes, and learning from what happens. in fact just finding out why someone won't buy what you made is a pretty good education on its own

> room to follow whatever he's obsessed with.

if he's into rockets, use that to teach him physics and math. help him build one. i want him to experience how exciting learning can be when you actually care about the thing you're trying to figure out.

> good human teachers who have time to actually get to know him.

people who notice when he's frustrated, challenge him when he's taking the easy way out, and introduce him to things he wouldn't have discovered on his own.

> a LOT of time around other kids.

yes, AI will make homeschooling incredibly good academically. but a huge part of school is learning how to be around other humans.

making friends, disagreeing without being an asshole, learning humility ,surviving embarassing moments. you have to actually live through that stuff

i'm hoping we have a lot more schools like this to choose from by the time he's old enough!

2102781855841788023.text:
On what made pg great, c. 2009-2016:

- every person tends toward particular kinds of ideas. Someone might tilt toward ideas that are entertaining, or elegant, or useful. Pg tended toward ideas that are surprising. He would look for surprising observations, generate surprising hypotheses, select surprising inferences. He'd never put it this way, but he seemed to find a lot of alpha in surprise
- pg was averse to abstractions. He almost always preferred a concrete way of doing things. Investors might ask about products or markets or business models. Pg would ask "what are you building?", "who is it for?", "how much will you charge?" It's the same questions, but he'd be as concrete and plain as possible
- being a hacker, he made things. His ideas were always practical and embodied in books, essays, software, YC, etc. They were meant to be used. It's very difficult to imagine pg writing a treatise on ethics or the nature of time or smtg
- this ethos is very much from Unix/C school of thought. Ironically, Pg was a Common Lisp hacker who embodied the worse-is-better philosophy. He would find the minimal possible thing that solves the problem, and it would be unmistakingly pg-esque. (If you haven't read The Rise of Worse is Better essay you should. Will the thesis be relitigated as AIs get much better?)
- that said, I'm not entirely sure he himself cared about making something people want. His output seems like an exhaust product of his curiosity that turned out to be useful by accident. Then again, he just couldn't help himself but stumble upon such accidents. Perhaps his way of thinking produces things people want, so for pg the score takes care of itself. The rest of us have to work at it deliberately
- he delighted in his ideas. The word "arrogance" has negative connotations, but pg was arrogant in the best possible way. If he thought an idea or an argument is good, it filled him with delight. It would then go into canon and he had no interest in revisiting it. There was no moving him once that happened
- the slop version of this is he "trusted his process" but again he would never put it this way. I don't think he was capable of navel gazing. It's impossible to imagine pg considering whether he'd be a favorite of fortune, or what posterity will think of him, or what he thinks of himself. In pg, the brain cycles most people spend on this would go to object level ideas
- I never saw the slightest sign he cares about what people think of him, nor did I ever see him try to impress anyone. I don't think he suppressed this impulse by force of will; as best as I could tell he has no such impulse. There is a Conversations with Tyler episode where pg keeps answering "I don't know" to a series of erudite questions without any embarrassment whatsoever. This is very pg
- he was interested in you if he thought you're smart and ambitious. If you did something to disabuse him of this, he'd lose interest completely. But this was never permanent; if you showed evidence of being smart and ambitious again his interest would rekindle. (You only got so many strikes, though) This brought out greatness in ppl because they would try very hard to impress him
- at the same time he genuinely cared about people's wellbeing. There are many stories where ppl had trouble in their personal life and he'd extend himself to help. I experienced some of this myself. Some values were much more important to him than ideas or ambition
- Thomas Jefferson once wrote "I am of a sect by myself", which I think sums up pg's character really well. If you read enough founding-father bios, you start noticing that most Silicon Valley figures resemble one founder more than the others. Imo pg is very much Jeffersonian

So almost every pre-AI B2B product we use has told us they are raising prices for agent access.

Salesforce and HubSpot are two of the latest, albeit differently (the price increases at HubSpot seem to be mainly for their own agents, while Saleforce is increasing prices for third party agents). But it’s not just them. Another niche CRM we’ve used for 5+ years just told us we have to pay extra for agent use of API.  Another niche product we use just deprecated the API we were using for 10K.

Maybe the only apps not doing this … are the ones that started agentic.

What I worry is the vendors aren’t thinking this through.

The immediate reaction of our agents to agentic price increases is … How Can We Work Around Them.

Not cheat.  But literally to move data off all these platforms so there is no API tax for the agents to use them.

And the humans naturally will want to stop having their agents use apps that raise steep prices to use them.

So I do worry these vendors are inadvertently creating an agentic death spiral.  Usage will drop, new agents will move off the platforms as much as practical, and these API tools will lead to less usage, less stickiness, and … less of a moat.

"I think a lot of starting startups is premature optimization. I see it in a lot of kids now, where they're part of a group and a lot of their friends are raising a lot of money, and some of them are becoming unicorns."

"The motivation becomes envy, a really negative motivation as opposed to a positive one."

"They pre-commit to an idea they're not even interested in, raise money for it, and start pre-optimizing for some path that they haven't really reached yet. That's why I always come back to this idea of curiosity. What is actually driving you?"

"Once you find that idea that you want to dedicate your life to, or dedicate the next 10 years to, it's going to have such gravity that you're not going to be able to avoid it."

"I actively tried not to start Replit, but it exploded into a startup on its own. That's the feeling you should get: 'I guess I have to do it,' because there's so much momentum behind it."

"There's a predatory thing I've heard that happens right now where VCs go to Stanford students and give them a million dollars pre-idea... It's like the music industry... You're taking this young person and pre-committing them to something they shouldn't have committed to."

@amasad

Introducing Contrastive Language Model (CLM): an ultra-fast System One Model trained with a contrastive learning objective that connects states and actions.

CLM-8B is pre-trained on internet-scale data and delivers up to 9× faster inference than Jev ⚡ while achieving comparable performance across computer-use, gaming, and tool-calling tasks.

Let me explain what just happened.

Anthropic built a biology lab where Claude works alongside real scientists.

They told Claude to search a massive DNA database for interesting reverse transcriptases (enzymes that copy RNA into DNA). Then they let it run: ~950 Claude agents worked in parallel for 21 hours across 200,000+ enzymes.

One agent spotted a repeating DNA pattern next to an enzyme, the same kind of signature that originally led humans to discover CRISPR (the gene-editing tool that lets scientists precisely cut and edit DNA, now used in real medical treatments). It cross-checked the pattern against known systems, searched the literature, confirmed nobody had found it before, then wrote up a full scientific report like a human researcher would.

Anthropic scientists verified it in the lab. They named it ART. Its exact function is still unknown, but early signs suggest it may be programmable, similar to how CRISPR can be aimed at specific DNA.

Why it matters: finding tools like CRISPR used to take human experts months of manual searching. Here, AI did that work and found something real, at a speed no human team could match.

So don't misunderstand it as Claude curing cancer. Claude spotted something new in nature that humans missed.

Still crazy!

Cold email got us zero customers.

Replying to strangers' posts instead is now 21% of our signups.

Personalization is pretty much worthless. The moment every founder can generate 10,000 "personalized" emails a day, mentioning a company name and a funding round stops being personalization.

The buyers today aren't in the inbox anyway. They're on Reddit asking or researching "what do you use for X." They're on Hacker News complaining their tool doubled its price. They're on X describing your product's problem in public.

The playbook:
1. Track conversations, not just your brand. Competitor names, category terms too.
2. Answer the question first, say who you are. No second accounts, no manufactured mentions.
3. Don't mention your product every time.
4. The founder replies for highest effectiveness.

Not counted in that 21%: signups from AI assistants, whose recommendations are built on the same public conversations.

It doesn't scale like an email sequence. But a sequence reaches a crowded inbox, this reaches someone actually thinking about the problem.
